text: The following question stood in the name of  Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry –  3  To ask the Minister for Finance what are the efforts to review cost efficiency of our large-scale infrastructure projects.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: asked the Minister for Finance what are the specific measures in place to ensure that costs are judiciously managed in the construction of large infrastructure projects, such as Changi Terminal 5, Tuas Mega Port and the Jurong Lake District.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are comprehensive measures in place to ensure the cost efficiency of publicly funded infrastructure projects, with greater scrutiny on projects that are of higher value or risk.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To help MOF perform this role, the Centre for Public Project Management (CP2M) was set up in 2011 with a multidisciplinary team of architects, engineers and quantity surveyors who review the scope, design and cost reasonableness of the proposals.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Changes may be made to revise the project scope or optimise the project design to achieve greater value-for-money.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: After the project passes the review by MOF, approval must be obtained from the Development Planning Committee (DPC), which comprises three Cabinet Ministers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This includes projects like Changi Terminal 5 (T5) and Tuas Port.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Such projects undergo a few stages of reviews by the Development Projects Advisory Panel (DPAP) supported by CP2M, before they are submitted to the DPC for approval.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: DPAP comprises senior public officers, academics and industry practitioners with deep technical expertise and experience in major infrastructure developments.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This allows us to draw on the expertise and best practices in both the public and private sectors.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The first stage of review assesses the strategic business case of the project and allows MOF and DPAP to be involved upstream in project planning.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The second stage seeks to refine and optimise the overall design, including the space take-up, construction method and procurement approach, to achieve greater value-for-money.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Gateway Process also allows agencies to work with DPAP to come up with alternative solutions that can achieve better or similar outcomes at lower costs over its lifecycle.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The measures to manage large infrastructure project costs do not end at project approval.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When a tender is called by the project agency, this is usually done through competitive open tender which allows price discovery.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There is also a robust assessment of the cost-benefit tradeoff before an award decision is made by the tender approving authority, which typically comprises senior officials.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, the award decisions for large infrastructure contracts called by the Land Transport Authority are approved by its governing Board.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The agency involved is required to provide justifications for the changes, which are scrutinised again by MOF before seeking re-approval from DPC.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Should the public be interested to track the yearly outlay on these mega infrastructure projects, how would they be able to see that in the yearly Budget release, given that the combined infrastructure spending budget for the Ministry of National Development (MND) and the Ministry of Transport (MOT) was only $15 billion in 2016, whereas the expected spending on these mega infrastructure projects are in the tens of billions?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, each year, you look at the relevant Ministries' budgets.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For mega projects, it is spread out but, typically, will be found in the budgets for MOT, MND and for the Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If the Member is asking whether the Budget Book sets out the expenditure in the next 15 or 20 years, you will not get that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What you will get is the expenditure for that year, but you can track it on a yearly basis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A point of clarification for the Senior Minister of State in view of the comments made yesterday about the funding of T5 and the views of the International Air Transport Association (IATA) that T5 should not be pre-funded with taxes or a tax levied on passengers, for example.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does the Ministry have any position on this?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Sorry, can I just check: when the Member referred to comments yesterday, whose comments yesterday?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Or was he referring to The Straits Times report this morning, I think?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It was also reported today in The Straits Times, and I believe it was a senior official of IATA who made those comments.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think what the official had commented on was something about how you should not have pre-funding.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Is that what the Member is referring to?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in short, we will try and find the most optimal way to do the funding and spread it out over the proper period of time.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I was wondering, in terms of cost efficiency, to what extent is the lifetime maintenance cost of a large infrastructure project considered as part of that efficiency, given that these projects may last many years and the design of the project may impact the ongoing cost required to upkeep and maintain it for future years.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is a very valid and pertinent question, and it is something that MOF is studying.
